sections.title: Computer: definition; data, information and program; hardware and software
Working principle of a computer: the IPOS cycle
Characteristics of a computer
Limitations of a computer and its effects on society
Uses of computers in Nepal

summary: A computer (Latin computare, to calculate) is an electronic machine that accepts data, processes it under a program, stores it and gives information.
Data are raw facts; information is processed, meaningful data. A program is a set of instructions; software is a collection of programs.
Hardware is the physical, touchable part; software tells it what to do. Neither works without the other.
IPOS: input devices → CPU (control unit + arithmetic logic unit) → output devices, with storage (RAM temporary, secondary storage permanent) joined to the CPU.
Characteristics: speed (ms, μs, ns), accuracy (GIGO), diligence, versatility, storage (8 bits = 1 byte, 1024 bytes = 1 KB) and automation.
Limitations: no IQ, no feelings, needs a program, correct input and electricity. Effects on society are both positive and negative.
Uses in Nepal: education, banking, health, communication, agriculture and government (Nagarik App, e-passport, National ID).

summary: Manual devices: abacus (c. 2700 BC; suanpan: heaven beads 5, earth beads 1), Napier's bones (John Napier, 1617; multiplication), slide rule (William Oughtred, c. 1622; analog).
Mechanical calculators: Pascaline (Blaise Pascal, 1642; add and subtract, automatic carry), stepped reckoner (Leibniz, 1673; all four operations), Jacquard loom (1804; punched cards as instructions).
Charles Babbage, father of the computer: Difference Engine (1822) and Analytical Engine (1834) with input cards, mill, store and output. Ada Lovelace wrote the first published program (1843).
Electromechanical: Hollerith's tabulator (1890 census; IBM, 1924), Harvard Mark I (Aiken and IBM, 1944).
Electronic: ABC (1942, first electronic digital), ENIAC (1946, first general-purpose; 17,468 tubes), EDVAC (stored program, binary), UNIVAC I (1951, first commercial in the USA).
Nepal: IBM 1401 rented in 2028 BS for the census; EDPC 2031 BS (later NCC); ICL 2950/10 in 2038 BS; microcomputers from 2039 BS.

sections.title: Meaning of a computer generation
First generation: vacuum tubes (about 1946–1958)
Second generation: transistors (about 1958–1964)
Third generation: integrated circuits (about 1964–1975)
Fourth generation: microprocessors (about 1975 to the present)
Fifth generation: artificial intelligence and parallel processing

summary: A generation is a stage of computer development marked by a major new technology, especially a new processing component; each generation is smaller, faster, cheaper, more reliable and more powerful.
1st (1946–1958): vacuum tubes, magnetic drums, machine language, milliseconds; huge, hot, unreliable. ENIAC, UNIVAC I.
2nd (1958–1964): transistors (Bell Labs, 1947), magnetic core memory, assembly language, FORTRAN and COBOL, microseconds. IBM 1401 (Nepal), IBM 7090.
3rd (1964–1975): integrated circuits (Kilby, 1958; Noyce, 1959), keyboards and monitors, time-sharing, BASIC and C, nanoseconds. IBM System/360.
4th (1975–present): microprocessors (Intel 4004, 1971; LSI, VLSI, ULSI), PCs, GUI, networks and the Internet. IBM PC, laptops, smartphones.
5th: artificial intelligence and parallel processing; natural language, learning machines, quantum research.
Moore's law: transistors on a chip double about every two years.

sections.title: Classification by working principle: analog, digital and hybrid computers

Microcomputers: desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone and workstation
Classification by purpose: general-purpose and special-purpose computers

summary: By working principle: analog computers measure continuous data (thermometer, speedometer, slide rule); digital computers count discrete data in 0s and 1s (PC, phone, calculator); hybrid computers do both (ECG, ICU monitor, petrol-pump dispenser).

By size: supercomputer (fastest; exaflops; weather, research — e.g. LineShine, Frontier), mainframe (thousands of users; banks, airlines — IBM z17), minicomputer (medium, multi-user — PDP-11; now servers), microcomputer (one user; microprocessor; PC).
Microcomputers: desktop, laptop (notebook), tablet, smartphone and workstation (powerful, for design and video).
By purpose: general-purpose computers run many programs; special-purpose computers do one job; one built into a machine is an embedded system.
Choosing a computer depends on the task and software, power, storage, portability, number of users and budget.

sections.title: Software: meaning and importance; how hardware and software work together

Installing, updating and removing software safely

summary: Software is a set of programs that tells the hardware what to do; it makes the computer usable, versatile and useful. It works in layers: user → application → operating system → device driver → hardware.
System software manages the computer: the operating system, device drivers (one for each device), utility programs (antivirus, backup, compression, disk cleanup) and language processors.
Assembler: assembly → machine code. Compiler: whole program at once, separate file, fast. Interpreter: line by line, stops at the first error.
Application software does the user's tasks: packaged (ready-made for many users — Word, Chrome, VLC) or tailor-made (built for one organization — a school's result system).
Licences: proprietary (buy; code secret), freeware (free; code secret), shareware (free trial, then pay), open source (free; code open to change and share). Piracy is illegal.
Install only from official sources, check requirements, keep software updated, and remove programs with Uninstall, not by deleting icons.

sections.title: Operating system: meaning and functions
Types of operating system: single-user and multi-user, CUI and GUI, desktop and mobile

Working with Windows: desktop, taskbar, Start menu, windows and dialog boxes
File management: files, folders, paths and extensions; copy, move, rename and delete; Recycle Bin

summary: An operating system manages all hardware and software and provides the user interface. Functions: process, memory, file and device management, security, user interface, booting.

Single-user (one user at a time — Windows 11 Home) vs multi-user (many at once — Linux servers). CUI (typed commands — MS-DOS, Linux terminal) vs GUI (windows, icons, menus, pointer — Windows, Android). Desktop OS (Windows, macOS, Linux) vs mobile OS (Android, iOS).
Windows (Microsoft, proprietary), Linux (Torvalds 1991, open source; Ubuntu, Fedora), macOS (Apple Macs), Android (Google, Linux-based, most-used mobile OS), iOS (iPhone).

Windows parts: desktop, icons, taskbar (Start, Search, apps, notification area, clock), Start menu, window (title bar, minimize/maximize/close, scroll bars, status bar), dialog box (tabs, text box, list, check box, option button, OK/Cancel/Apply).
A file has a name and an extension (.docx, .jpg, .exe); a folder holds files; a path gives the full address, e.g. D:\School\Grade 8\summary.docx.

Copy (Ctrl + C, Ctrl + V) keeps the original; move (Ctrl + X, Ctrl + V) does not; rename with F2. Delete sends to the Recycle Bin (restore or empty); Shift + Delete and pen-drive deletions are permanent.
Settings (Win + I): time zone (UTC+05:45) Kathmandu, display, user accounts (administrator or standard), Apps → Installed apps to uninstall.

summary: A word processor creates, edits, formats, saves and prints documents: Microsoft Word, LibreOffice Writer, Google Docs. Features include word wrap, find and replace, spell check, tables, pictures and mail merge.
Word's window: title bar, Quick Access Toolbar, ribbon (tabs → groups → commands), ruler, document area, insertion point, scroll bars, status bar.
New Ctrl + N, Open Ctrl + O, Save Ctrl + S (Save As F12 makes a new copy), Print Ctrl + P with copies, pages (1-3, 6) and sides; DOCX for Word, ODT for Writer, PDF for sharing.
Editing: select, Cut Ctrl + X (move), Copy Ctrl + C, Paste Ctrl + V, Undo Ctrl + Z, Find Ctrl + F, Replace Ctrl + H (match case, whole words), spelling and grammar F7.

Formatting: font, size (points), bold/italic/underline; alignment (Ctrl + L/E/R/J), line spacing, indents; bullets and numbering; margins (Normal 2.54 cm), orientation, A4 size; header (top), footer (bottom), page numbers (Insert → Page Number).
Objects: tables (rows × columns = cells; merge, split), pictures (Wrap Text), shapes and WordArt (Writer: Fontwork).
Mail merge = main document + data source → one merged copy per row (Mailings → Start Mail Merge → Select Recipients → Insert Merge Field → Preview → Finish & Merge).

summary: A spreadsheet (Excel, Calc, Google Sheets) calculates with data in rows and columns. A workbook (.xlsx, .ods) holds worksheets; a cell is where a row (number) meets a column (letter); its address is like C5; a range is written B2:E6 and has columns × rows cells.
Data types: text (left), numbers (right), currency, percentage, dates, formulas, TRUE/FALSE. Errors: #####, #DIV/0!, #NAME?, #VALUE!, #REF!. AutoFill with the fill handle copies or continues series.
Formulas start with =; operators + - * / ^ %, comparisons = <> > < >= <=, &; brackets first, then ^, then × ÷, then + −.
Relative references (B2) change when copied; absolute (B1) do not; mixed B1, B1; F4 toggles.
Functions: SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT (numbers only), IF(condition, if_true, if_false); nested IF for grades.
Formatting (Ctrl + 1) changes appearance, not values; sort the whole table (Data → Sort); filter hides rows (Data → Filter).
Charts: column and bar compare items, line shows change over time, pie shows parts of a whole (angle = share × 360°).

summary: Presentation software (PowerPoint, Impress, Google Slides, Keynote, Canva) creates and shows slides; files are .pptx or .odp.

A layout arranges placeholders on a slide (Title Slide, Title and Content, Two Content, Comparison, Title Only, Picture with Caption); a theme designs all slides; a placeholder holds a title, text or object.
New slide Ctrl + M; insert pictures, tables, charts, audio and video from the Insert tab; the Playback tab sets how audio and video start.
A transition works between slides (Transitions tab, Apply To All, Advance After); an animation works on objects (entrance, emphasis, exit, motion paths; On Click, With Previous, After Previous).
Views: Normal, Outline, Slide Sorter, Notes Page, Reading View, Slide Show. The slide master changes every slide at once.
Show: F5 from the beginning, Shift + F5 from the current slide, Esc to end; Presenter View for the speaker.
Effective slides: one idea per slide, 6 × 6 rule, large type, strong contrast, consistent design, few animations, rehearse.

summary: ICT is the use of computers, telecommunication equipment, networks and software to collect, store, process, send and receive information.
Its six components are hardware, software, data, network, people and procedures.

Communication technologies: telephone (voice over wire), mobile (radio waves to the tower of each cell), radio (one-way sound), television (one-way pictures and sound), satellite (uplink and downlink; geostationary at about 35,786 km) and the Internet (a network of networks that carries everything).
Nepal's milestones: Radio Nepal 1951, NTV 1985, e-mail 1994, first ISP 1995, GSM mobile 1999, 4G 2017, NepaliSat-1 2019, Nagarik App 2021.
Internet services: WWW (linked web pages; not the same as the Internet), e-mail (To, Cc, Bcc, attachment), search engines, chat, video conferencing and cloud storage.

ICT in Nepal: e-governance (G2C, G2B, G2G; Nagarik App), online banking and digital payments (eSewa, Khalti, Fonepay QR, connectIPS; never share an OTP or MPIN) and e-learning (Sikai Chautari, E-Paath).
The digital divide is the gap between those who have devices, the Internet and the skill to use them and those who do not; in 2021, 45.7% of urban but 21.5% of rural households had Internet.

sections.title: Computer ethics: meaning and the Ten Commandments of computer ethics
Cyber crime: hacking, phishing, cyber bullying, identity theft and software piracy
Intellectual property, copyright and plagiarism
Cyber law in Nepal: the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063
Digital citizenship and safe use of social media

summary: Computer ethics are the moral rules for using computers; laws are enforced by the state. Every cyber crime is unethical, but not every unethical act is a crime.
The Ten Commandments (Computer Ethics Institute, 1992): do not harm, interfere, snoop, steal, lie, copy paid software, use others' resources or take others' work; think about society; respect others.
Cyber crime is any illegal act done with a computer or the Internet: hacking, phishing, cyber bullying, identity theft, software piracy, online fraud.

Intellectual property is protected by copyright, patents, trademarks and designs. In Nepal copyright lasts for the author's life plus 50 years (Copyright Act, 2059); plagiarism is using work without credit.
Nepal's cyber law is the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063, authenticated 22 Mansir 2063 (8 December 2006): 12 chapters, 80 sections, offences in sections 44–59.

Key punishments: s.44 source code and s.45 unauthorised access and s.46 damage — up to Rs 2 lakh or 3 years or both; s.47 illegal material — up to Rs 1 lakh or 5 years or both; s.52 fraud — Rs 1 lakh or 2 years or both. Report to the Cyber Bureau of Nepal Police.
A digital citizen follows netiquette, protects privacy, uses strong passwords and MFA, thinks before posting, checks facts and manages a digital footprint (active and passive).

sections.title: Computer virus: meaning, history and how it spreads
Types of malware: virus, worm, Trojan horse, spyware, adware and ransomware
Symptoms of an infected computer
Antivirus software: how it works and examples
Protecting a computer: safe browsing, updates, backups and strong passwords

summary: A computer virus is a harmful program that attaches itself to files, copies itself when the file is run, and damages data without the user's knowledge; malware is the general name for all harmful programs.
History: Creeper (1971), Elk Cloner (1982), the name "computer virus" by Fred Cohen (1983–84), Brain from Lahore (1986, first PC virus), Morris worm (1988), ILOVEYOU (2000), WannaCry (2017).
Viruses spread through pen drives, pirated software, e-mail attachments, fake links and apps, and networks.

Types: virus (needs a host; boot sector, file, macro, multipartite), worm (spreads by itself over networks), Trojan horse (disguised as useful), spyware (secretly watches; keyloggers), adware (unwanted adverts), ransomware (locks files for money).
Symptoms: slowness, crashes, missing or locked files, shortcut folders on pen drives, pop-ups, a disabled antivirus, messages sent without you.

Antivirus detects, blocks and removes malware by signature checking, behaviour checking and real-time scanning, then cleans, quarantines or deletes; it must be updated. Examples: Microsoft Defender, Avast, Kaspersky, Norton, ClamAV. A firewall guards the network, an antivirus the files.
Protection: antivirus and firewall, automatic updates, safe browsing and downloads, scanning pen drives, the 3-2-1 backup rule, strong unique passwords with MFA, and standard user accounts.

sections.title: Computer network: meaning, advantages and disadvantages
Network components: server, client, NIC, cables, hub, switch, router and modem
Transmission media: wired and wireless
Types of network: LAN, MAN and WAN

The internet as a network of networks

summary: A computer network is two or more computers and devices connected by wired or wireless media to share data, hardware, software and an Internet connection; every device on it is a node, and all follow protocols.

Advantages: sharing hardware, data and one Internet line; fast communication; central control and backup. Disadvantages: cost and skill, fast spread of viruses, security risk, dependence on the server or switch.

Components: server (provides services), client (uses them), NIC (with a 48-bit MAC address), cables, hub (copies to all ports), switch (sends only to the destination port, by MAC address), router (joins networks, by IP address), modem (digital ↔ analog; ONT on fibre), Wi-Fi access point.

Wired media: twisted pair (UTP, RJ-45, 100 m), coaxial (cable TV), optical fibre (light, fastest, many km). Wireless media: radio and Wi-Fi, Bluetooth (about 10 m), microwave (line of sight), satellite, infrared.
LAN (building, up to about 1 km, fastest), MAN (city or valley), WAN (country or world; the Internet); PAN (one person, about 10 m). WLAN is a wireless LAN, not a WAN.
Topologies: bus (one backbone, terminators, one break stops all), ring (closed loop, one direction, token), star (own cable to a central switch; most common; the centre is the weak point).
The Internet is a network of networks joined by routers and TCP/IP; data travels in packets with IP addresses; ISPs meet at npIX; ARPANET began in 1969 and Nepal got the Internet in 1995.
Speed is in bits per second: divide Mbps by 8 to get MB per second.

summary: A number system writes numbers with a fixed set of digits; its base (radix) is the number of digits, and the largest digit is base − 1. Binary (2: 0, 1), octal (8: 0–7), decimal (10: 0–9), hexadecimal (16: 0–9, A–F with A = 10 … F = 15). Always write the base: (101)2.
All four are positional: place values are powers of the base, starting with base^0 = 1 at the right.

Computers use binary because their switches have two states (off/on); octal (3 bits per digit) and hexadecimal (4 bits per digit) are short ways of writing binary — hex is used for colour codes and MAC addresses.
Decimal → any base: divide by the base until the quotient is 0; read the remainders from the bottom up; write 10–15 as A–F.
Any base → decimal: multiply each digit by its place value and add.
Binary → octal / hex: group bits in threes / fours from the right, padding 0s on the left. Octal / hex → binary: write 3 / 4 bits for each digit. Octal ↔ hex: go through binary.
Memory: bit; nibble = 4 bits; byte = 8 bits; KB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB, ZB, YB, each 1024 times the one before. Disk makers and network speeds use 1000.

summary: Computer graphics are pictures, drawings, charts and animations made, stored, edited and shown by computer; they may be 2D or 3D, interactive or non-interactive. Uses: design, advertising, entertainment, education, CAD, maps, medicine, charts and the GUI.
Raster (bitmap) graphics are grids of pixels; resolution is width × height in pixels; colour depth n bits gives 2^n colours (24-bit = 16,777,216). Uncompressed size = width × height × bits ÷ 8 bytes.
Each pixel's colour is a mix of red, green and blue, each 0–255.
Vector graphics store shapes as numbers and stay sharp at any size; raster pictures pixelate when enlarged.
Paint (raster, with Windows), GIMP (free raster editor, XCF, layers), Inkscape (free vector editor, SVG) and Canva (online templates, free and Pro plans).
Paint tools: select, crop, resize and skew, rotate/flip, pencil, fill, text, eraser, colour picker, magnifier, brushes, shapes, size, Colour 1 and 2.
BMP uncompressed; JPEG lossy, photos; PNG lossless, transparency; GIF 256 colours, animation; SVG vector.

summary: Multimedia is the combined use of two or more media — text, graphics, audio, video and animation — usually with a computer.
Video is recorded from real life with a camera; animation is drawn or computer-made pictures shown quickly (about 12–30 a second) so they seem to move.
Linear multimedia plays in a fixed order (a film); interactive multimedia responds to the user (E-Paath, games, websites).

Hardware: input — microphone, webcam, camera, scanner, graphics tablet; output — monitor, speakers, headphones, projector; inside — CPU, RAM, graphics card, sound card; storage — SSD, hard disk, memory card, cloud.
Software: VLC (player), Audacity (audio), OpenShot, Kdenlive and CapCut (video), Pencil2D and Blender (animation), GIMP and Inkscape (graphics), PowerPoint (presentation).
Uncompressed sound = samples per second × bits × channels × seconds ÷ 8 bytes; one minute of CD sound ≈ 10.1 MB, as MP3 ≈ 0.92 MB; MP4 makes video about a hundred times smaller.
Uses: education, entertainment, business, health (medical images, telemedicine); advantages and disadvantages as in the table.

summary: A program is a set of instructions in a programming language; programming is planning, writing, testing and correcting programs.
The program development life cycle: problem analysis (input, process, output), program design, coding, testing and debugging, documentation, implementation and maintenance.
An algorithm is a finite set of clear step-by-step instructions from Start to Stop; a good one has input, output, definiteness, finiteness and effectiveness.
A flowchart draws an algorithm with standard symbols: oval (start/stop), parallelogram (input/output), rectangle (process), diamond (decision), arrows (flow lines), circle (connector).
Flowchart rules: one Start and one Stop, top to bottom, arrows on every line, two labelled exits on every decision, no crossing lines.
Every algorithm is built from sequence, selection (decision, branching) and repetition (loop); a loop needs initialisation, a condition and an update, or it never ends.
Pseudocode is structured English with keywords (INPUT, PRINT, IF … ENDIF, WHILE … ENDWHILE, FOR … NEXT) that is easy to turn into a real program.
A trace table (dry run) follows an algorithm by hand to test it before coding.

summary: A programming language is a set of words, symbols and rules (syntax) for writing instructions for a computer.

Low-level languages: machine language (binary; runs directly; machine-dependent) and assembly language (mnemonics such as MOV and ADD; needs an assembler). High-level languages (Python, C, Java) are English-like and portable.

Language processors turn source code into object code: a compiler translates the whole program at once and makes an object program; an interpreter translates and runs one line at a time; an assembler translates assembly language.
Syntax error: breaking the rules of the language. Run-time error: an impossible operation while running, such as division by zero. Logical error: wrong method, wrong output, no message.
Testing runs a program with test data of known answers; debugging finds and corrects errors (error messages, dry runs, printing values, stepping with IDLE's debugger, breakpoints).
Python (Guido van Rossum, 1991), C (Dennis Ritchie, 1972), Java (James Gosling, Sun, 1995).

A constant never changes (numeric or string); a variable is a named memory location whose value can change; Python names use letters, digits and _, do not start with a digit, contain no spaces and are not keywords.
Python data types: int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text) and bool (True or False).

summary: Python (Guido van Rossum, 1991) is an easy, interpreted, case-sensitive language in which indentation matters. Programs are written in IDLE's editor, saved as .py and run with F5; the Shell's >>> prompt carries out one line at a time.

Character set: letters, digits, special characters and white space. Keywords have a fixed meaning and cannot be names. Identifiers use letters, digits and _, do not start with a digit, contain no spaces or special characters and are case-sensitive. A comment starts with #.
A variable is created by assignment (x = 5) and can change; a constant is written in capitals by custom. The basic data types are int, float, str and bool; type() shows a value's type.
Operators: arithmetic (+ - * / // % ), relational (== != > < >= <=), logical (and or not) and assignment (= += -= = /=). Order: brackets, , / // %, + -, comparisons, not, and, or. ^ is not power.
Output: print() with sep and end; \n and \t; f-strings with {value:.2f}. Input: input() always returns text, so convert it with int() or float().
Functions: abs, max, min, round, len; the math module (import math): sqrt, floor, ceil, pi; string indexing from 0, slices s[a:b], upper(), lower(), count().
Selection: if, if … else, if … elif … else and nested if; colon and indentation are essential; the first true branch runs.

Loops: for with range(start, stop, step) (the stop is not reached; a negative step counts down) and while (tested before each pass); break leaves a loop; nested loops make tables and patterns. Start a sum at 0 and a product at 1.
